source_title: The Archimede Rover: A Comparison between Simulations and Experiments (Caruso, Giberna, Gorner, Gallina, Seriani; Robotics 12(5), 125, 2023)
evidence_row: SIM-030 (same source, other finding)
x_name: slope angle of the tilted sandbox (nominal, 5 deg steps)
y_name: slip s (median of all drive tests at that slope and wheel speed)
vehicle: Archimede rover prototype, four independently steered and driven wheels, wheelbase 0.720 m, track 0.443 m, body 1.61 kg plus two legs of 1.58 kg (Table 1); commanded mean wheel speed 1.2 rad/s
soil: granular lava, grain size 1 to 5 mm (Test Setup A)
preparation: Planetary Exploration Laboratory sandbox with a tilting section, slope raised in 5 deg steps to 20 deg; drives in straight, lateral and parallel modes pooled; rover tracked by an optical tracking system
comparability_note: Each point is the median slip of all drive tests at that slope and wheel speed, pooling straight, lateral and parallel driving modes (Sec. 3.1.2, 4.2), so not every run is a straight ascent along the fall line. The y axis is labelled s [/] (fraction) although the caption says slip percentage; values are kept as plotted. How s is computed is not written out in Sec. 4.2. Seeds are marker bounding box centres; for the triangles, if the plotting software anchors the marker at the triangle centroid instead, values would be about 0.008 lower. x is the nominal sandbox slope; the actual slope tolerance is not reported. Table 1 prints the wheel diameters as 0.170 and 0.186 with unit mm, which must be metres given the 0.720 m wheelbase; wheel width and grouser height are not reported. load_per_wheel_N derived here from Table 1 masses (1.61 + 1.58 + 1.58 = 4.77 kg) times 9.81 divided by 4 wheels; the table note says the body mass in this work differs slightly. Setup A soil is granular lava of 1 to 5 mm, coarser than dune sand.

x_name: slope angle of the tilted sandbox (nominal, 5 deg steps)
y_name: slip s (median of all drive tests at that slope and wheel speed)
vehicle: Archimede rover prototype, four independently steered and driven wheels, wheelbase 0.720 m, track 0.443 m, body 1.61 kg plus two legs of 1.58 kg (Table 1); commanded mean wheel speed 2.4 rad/s
soil: EAC-1A lunar regolith simulant, very loose, submillimetre grains (Test Setup B)
preparation: Planetary Exploration Laboratory sandbox with a tilting section, slope raised in 5 deg steps to 20 deg; drives in straight, lateral and parallel modes pooled; rover tracked by an optical tracking system
comparability_note: Each point is the median slip of all drive tests at that slope and wheel speed, pooling straight, lateral and parallel driving modes (Sec. 3.1.2, 4.2), so not every run is a straight ascent along the fall line. The y axis is labelled s [/] (fraction) although the caption says slip percentage; values are kept as plotted. How s is computed is not written out in Sec. 4.2. Seeds are marker bounding box centres; for the triangles, if the plotting software anchors the marker at the triangle centroid instead, values would be about 0.008 lower. x is the nominal sandbox slope; the actual slope tolerance is not reported. Table 1 prints the wheel diameters as 0.170 and 0.186 with unit mm, which must be metres given the 0.720 m wheelbase; wheel width and grouser height are not reported. load_per_wheel_N derived here from Table 1 masses (1.61 + 1.58 + 1.58 = 4.77 kg) times 9.81 divided by 4 wheels; the table note says the body mass in this work differs slightly. EAC-1A is a basaltic lunar simulant, finer and more cohesive than quartz dune sand.

source_title: Effect of Angle of Attack on Slope Climbing Performance (Creager, Jones, Smith; NASA/TM 2017-219549, December 2017)
evidence_row: TM3-001 to TM3-007 (same source, other findings)
figure_or_table: Figure 11, angle of attack 10 deg (dark blue squares)
x_name: slope angle (actual, best fit plane of the surface point cloud)
vehicle: Scarab rover, 400 kg, four rigid wheels, active suspension not used (fixed chassis height and axle spacing), wheel speed 0.13 rad/s for 30 s
soil: GRC-1 lunar simulant sand mixture, loosened (Table 1: D60 0.390 mm, specific gravity 2.583, relative density 11 percent, cohesion about 0 kPa)
preparation: SLOPE laboratory tilt bed about 6 m by 4.5 m, GRC-1 23 cm deep, loosened before each test; mean cone index gradient 2.5 plus or minus 0.5 kPa/mm
slope_kind: angle of attack 10 deg to the slope base (90 is straight up)
comparability_note: Slip of the rear wheel averaged over each 30 s run from photogrammetric wheel tracking, i = 1 minus distance travelled over (effective radius times wheel rotation) in the direction the vehicle faced; front and rear differ by less than 0.5 percent (text). x values are the actual slope angles of each run read from the figure, single runs (no repeats). The 0 deg reference test, plotted at about minus 1 percent for all four series, is left out because the four markers overlap there. Markers found automatically as connected colour components after removing the connecting lines by morphological opening. load_per_wheel_N derived here as 400 kg times 9.81 divided by 4 wheels (the text says the load was fairly even on flat ground). GRC-1 is a manufactured sand mixture with lunar strength properties, wider graded than dune sand; very large and heavy wheels.

source_title: Improving Slip Prediction on Mars Using Thermal Inertia Measurements (Cunningham, Whittaker, Nesnas; Robotics: Science and Systems XIII, 2017, paper 38)
evidence_row: PLN-052 to PLN-055; MAP-023 to MAP-025 (same source, other findings)
figure_or_table: Figure 7, top panel (sand slip samples, coloured by THEMIS thermal inertia)
x_name: slope (rover tilt magnitude averaged over the drive from the IMU, positive when driving up the slope)
y_name: slip (mean of all wheel slips, longitudinal and lateral together, from visual odometry)
vehicle: MSL Curiosity rover, six wheel rocker bogie, about 3 m long
soil: aeolian sand and sand covered terrain classified from rover images (Hidden Valley, Moosilauke Valley, Logans Pass, Jubilee Pass, Ripple Crossing, Dingo Gap, Artists Drive), Gale crater, Mars
preparation: natural terrain, sols 1 to 986; visual odometry drives of 0.5 m or longer with at least four wheels on sand; 135 samples from 9 sites (Table I)
slope_kind: mixed (signed, ascent and descent; heading not restricted)
comparability_note: Points are medians of coloured marker pixels in 2 deg slope bins (pixel weighted, so roughly marker weighted, overlapping markers under counted; bins with fewer than 250 marker pixels, about one or two markers, are dropped, so the isolated samples near -14, 1.8 and 16 deg are not represented); x_unc and y_unc combine reading error with half the interquartile range in the bin. The scatter is bimodal at the same slope (low and high thermal inertia sand), so bin medians hide a spread of up to about 70 percent slip; treat the curve as a summary of field scatter, not as a single soil response. Slip y = (1 minus v over vref) times 100 when driving (Eq. 5); slip and slope are magnitudes of the vector (longitudinal plus lateral), with sign set by uphill or downhill driving, so this is not pure direct ascent. The bottom panel shows the same samples coloured by GTS thermal inertia and is not digitised again. Mars gravity 0.38 g, about 900 kg rover, basaltic sand.

vehicle: MGRU3 (Moon Gravitation Representative Unit 3) VIPER test rover, four wheels, on the SLOPE lab tilt bed
wheel_diameter_m: not reported for MGRU3 (the VIPER single wheel used in the lab is 0.50 m)

bulk_density_kg_m3: not reported for the tests (Fig. 4a shows a GRC-1 range of about 1600 to 1820)

preparation: not described in this source

Source plot has slip on x and slope on y; output x is slope and y is slip. Calibration on the light grey gridlines at slip 0 and 0.8 and slope 0 and 40 deg. The box centre of a left pointing triangle lies left of its centroid by about a sixth of its width (about 0.006 slip here). Gravity offset rover at 1 g; load per wheel about 216 N if the 88 kg twin mass applies (derived).

source_title: Discrete element method analysis of single wheel performance for a small lunar rover on sloped terrain (Nakashima, Fujii, Oida, Momozu, Kanamori, Aoki, Yokoyama, Shimizu, Miyasaka, Ohdoi; Journal of Terramechanics 47(5), 2010, 307 to 321)
evidence_row: not in evidence.csv
vehicle: single wheel dynamometer on a tilting soil bin (1.5 m by 2.0 m, simulant depth 0.1 m), aluminium lugged wheel
soil: lunar regolith simulant FJS-1 (specific gravity 2.94, cohesion 2.55 kPa from triaxial tests, Table 2)
bulk_density_kg_m3: 1480 (average dry bulk density from vane shear calibration at 4 cm depth; relative density 17.4 percent, loose)
preparation: simulant raked by hand, moved up and down in the bin and levelled with a plate before each run; bin then tilted to the slope angle; runs repeated twice
comparability_note: Markers found automatically as connected components of the red experiment markers after a morphological opening that removes the red dashed line; the DEM series (blue squares) and the legend are excluded. Source plot has slip on x and slope on y (swapped on output); the test design slopes were 0, 10, 15, 20 and 25 deg (Table 3) and the digitised slopes agree with them within 0.1 deg. The paper states that runs were repeated twice but does not say whether a marker is a mean. Slip i = 1 minus Vs/(rw omega) with rw taken as the outer radius including lug height (Eq. 2), so slip may be biased relative to a free rolling radius definition. The wheel load is constant at all slopes (counterweight), as stated. Wheel angular velocity in the experiments was 0.1, 0.2 or 0.3 rad/s (Table 3); which speed this curve used is not stated. FJS-1 is a crushed basaltic lunar simulant with cohesion, not quartz dune sand; slip at 1 g. The 0 deg experiment marker is mostly hidden under the DEM square and is left out (only a sliver at about 7 percent slip is visible).

source_title: Effects of wheel width on running performance of four-wheeled small lunar rover (Watanabe, Maru, Kawaguchi, Tanaka; Transactions of the JSME, in Japanese, Vol. 92, No. 956, 2026)
evidence_row: TM3-047; TM3-048; TM3-049 (same source, other findings)
vehicle: four wheeled small lunar rover, 3D printed ABS, 1.5 kg (ballasted to the same mass for every wheel set), wheelbase 200 mm, all wheels driven at 10 rpm
grousers: 12 lugs, 10 mm high, 3 mm thick, equally spaced
soil: FJS-1 lunar regolith simulant, about 110 mm deep
preparation: tilting simulant bed 2000 mm by 1000 mm, electric lift up to 37 deg; soil tilled from depth and levelled before each run; mean of 9 inclinometer readings on the course within 1 deg of the target; vane shear torque at 20 mm depth below 0.30 cNm
comparability_note: Each point is the mean of 5 runs over 700 mm (error bars 1 SD, not transcribed). Slip ratio by Eq. (1): 1 minus V over r omega when driving, with r the radius including lugs. x is the nominal slope set for the test; the text states the mean of 9 readings on the course was within 1 deg of it, so x_unc is 1 deg. y read from the marker of this wheel width, refined to the centroid of its colour; markers of the seven widths overlap at low slopes, so partly hidden markers were kept only when roughly half or more of the marker was visible, and fully hidden ones are left out (10 and 15 deg markers hidden; the rover stuck at 30 deg (text, Sec. 3.1), so no marker at 30 deg). Partial hiding can shift a centroid by up to the marker radius, which is the stated y_unc. load_per_wheel_N derived here as 1.5 kg times 9.81 divided by 4 wheels. Very light rover (1.5 kg) with narrow 3D printed wheels; the paper scales a 5 to 10 kg lunar rover to 1/6 mass, not to Earth sand traverses.
